tasks.name: Frame the problem and establish a correct baseline
Analyze work and remove the bottleneck
Preserve correctness and verify the solution

concepts.name: Interview reasoning signal
concepts.description: Make the problem-solving process visible: clarify requirements, state a plan, explain trade-offs, write correct code, and test it.

concepts.name: Correct baseline first
concepts.description: Start from a simple correct approach before optimizing so correctness and the real bottleneck are explicit.

concepts.name: Repeatable interview workflow
concepts.description: Use a stable fallback loop: clarify, example, baseline, bottleneck, invariant/complexity, code, and test.

concepts.name: Asymptotic growth
concepts.description: Use Big O to describe how time or extra space grows with input size and to reject approaches that do not scale to the stated constraints.

concepts.name: Count aggregate operations
concepts.description: Analyze how many times the expensive operation can occur overall instead of judging complexity from loop nesting alone.

concepts.name: Brute force to bottleneck
concepts.description: Improve a correct baseline by identifying repeated expensive work and maintaining or precomputing the information that removes it.

concepts.name: Invariant and progress
concepts.description: State what remains true as the algorithm runs and verify that each update preserves that condition while making progress toward termination.

concepts.name: Boundary and counterexample testing
concepts.description: Use small boundary cases and counterexamples to expose off-by-one errors, missing cases, invalid assumptions, and no-solution behavior.

questions.prompt: A prompt says: “Given a sequence of IDs, return whether any ID repeats.” Which clarifications can materially change the solution or its contract?
questions.explanation: Input scale can change what complexity is practical; mutation rules can rule out sorting in place; memory limits can change whether extra state is acceptable. Variable names do not change the algorithmic contract.
hints: Ask whether the answer or implementation would change if this detail changed.

error_codes.description: At least one relevant clarification was missed.
At least one irrelevant clarification was selected.

questions.prompt: Put the fallback interview workflow in a useful order.
questions.explanation: The order deliberately makes correctness visible before optimization: clarify the contract, test a tiny example, state a correct baseline, identify its bottleneck, state the invariant/complexity, then code and test.
hints: Do not optimize before you have a correct approach to analyze.

error_codes.description: One or more workflow steps are out of order.

questions.prompt: You need to detect whether a list contains a duplicate, but the interviewer has not given useful size constraints yet. Which opening explanation is the strongest baseline?
questions.explanation: A pairwise comparison is simple and correct, so it gives you a concrete O(n²) baseline. You can then identify repeated membership/search work and optimize deliberately.
hints: Choose the explanation that is obviously correct before worrying about the final optimization.

error_codes.description: The selected opening skips or weakens the correct-baseline reasoning.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

choice_feedback.pairwise: Good baseline: it is easy to justify as correct, and its cost is visible.
choice_feedback.sort_now: Sorting may be useful, but it assumes reordering is acceptable and skips the baseline reasoning.
choice_feedback.binary_search: Binary search is not valid on unsorted input without additional work.
choice_feedback.hash_magic: A hash set may be a strong optimization, but jumping there without explaining the baseline hides the bottleneck-removal reasoning this step is practicing.

choices.label: “I can first compare each pair. That is correct but O(n²); then I’ll see whether the repeated search can be removed.”

“I remember this is a hash-set question, so I’ll code that without discussing a baseline.”

questions.prompt:
What is the time complexity of this code as a function of n = len(values)?

`total = 0`
`for value in values:`
`    total += value`
questions.explanation: The loop performs a bounded amount of work for each of n values, so the time grows linearly: O(n).
hints: Count how many times the addition executes as n grows.

error_codes.description: The selected growth rate does not match the number of operations.

choice_feedback.o1: The number of additions grows with n.
choice_feedback.ologn: Nothing is halving the remaining work.
choice_feedback.on: Correct: one bounded-cost update per input item.
choice_feedback.on2: There is no all-pairs or repeated full scan.

choices.label: O(log n)
O(n)

questions.prompt: Classify each code shape by its dominant asymptotic time.
questions.explanation: Constant work is O(1); repeatedly halving a remaining quantity is O(log n); a single full scan is O(n); an all-pairs nested scan is O(n²).
hints: Focus on how many times the body can run as n grows.

error_codes.description: At least one code shape was matched to the wrong growth rate.

questions.prompt: A duplicate detector compares every value with every later value. Which observations identify the actual bottleneck?
questions.explanation: The expensive behavior is not the variable assignment or return. It is the repeated pair comparison/search: many items trigger many later comparisons.
hints: Ask which operation is repeated enough times to dominate the running time.

error_codes.description: Part of the repeated expensive work was missed.
A low-cost operation was mistaken for the dominant bottleneck.

questions.prompt: Flag the incorrect complexity claim. In every loop iteration exactly one of `left` or `right` increases, and neither pointer ever decreases.
questions.explanation: Even if the control flow looks like two moving loops or branches, left can advance at most n times and right at most n times. The total number of pointer advances is at most 2n, which is O(n).
hints: Count the total number of pointer increments across the whole run.

error_codes.description: The incorrect loop-shape complexity claim was not identified.
A correct aggregate-work statement was incorrectly flagged.

questions.prompt: Which TWO code patterns can create O(n²) work when performed for each of n input items?
questions.explanation: A full list membership scan and `list.index` are both linear in the list length; placing either inside another n-scale loop can produce quadratic work. Constant arithmetic and one pre-loop sort do not have that shape.
hints: Look for an O(n)-scale operation repeated O(n) times.

error_codes.description: One repeated linear operation was missed.
A non-quadratic shape was selected.
The selected pair does not match repeated O(n) work.

questions.explanation: Optimization should follow the cost: establish correctness, identify the dominant repeated operation, identify reusable information, choose state/data structure, restate complexity, then re-check correctness.

questions.prompt: A service processes n event IDs once. The baseline checks each new ID by scanning all previously seen IDs. Which change most directly removes the repeated expensive operation?
questions.explanation: The repeated cost is rescanning earlier IDs for membership. Maintaining a hash-based set stores the exact information being recomputed and supports expected constant-time membership operations under the usual hashing model.

error_codes.description: The selected change does not remove the repeated membership scan.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 4: Hashing

choice_feedback.set: Correct: it directly replaces repeated membership scans with maintained membership state.
choice_feedback.rename: Renaming variables does not change the dominant operation.
choice_feedback.reverse: Reversing the data preserves the same repeated scanning cost.
choice_feedback.copy: Copying the list adds work without eliminating the repeated membership scan.

choices.label: Maintain a hash-based set of IDs already seen
Use shorter variable names in the nested scan
Reverse the input before running the same nested scan
Copy the input before checking duplicates

questions.prompt:
Before each iteration of this loop, `i` is the number of values already processed. Which statement is the strongest loop invariant?

`total = 0`
`for i, value in enumerate(values):`
`    total += value`
questions.explanation: The useful invariant describes the exact relationship between state and processed input: before processing index i, total equals the sum of values before i.
hints: An invariant should be precise enough to connect the maintained variable to the processed part of the input.

error_codes.description: The selected statement is not the useful processed-prefix invariant.

source_refs.title: Cornell CS 2112 — Loop invariants

choice_feedback.prefix: Correct: it precisely connects total to the already-processed prefix.
choice_feedback.positive: The input values do not have to be positive.
choice_feedback.final: The final result is not generally available before every iteration.
choice_feedback.changes: An invariant is a stable relationship, not merely the fact that a variable changes.

choices.label: `total` equals the sum of all values processed before the current iteration
`total` is always positive
`total` already equals the final sum
`total` changes on every iteration

questions.prompt: The input is sorted. The search uses an inclusive interval `[left, right]`. Flag the update that can fail to make progress when `mid == left`.
questions.explanation: `left = mid` can leave left unchanged, so the candidate interval may never shrink. When `values[mid] < target`, mid is known not to be the target, so `left = mid + 1` both preserves the candidate invariant and makes progress.
hints: Try a two-element interval where mid evaluates to left.

error_codes.description: The non-progressing boundary update was not identified.
A valid search step was incorrectly flagged.

source_refs.title: Cornell CS 2112 — Loop invariants

questions.prompt: In an inclusive binary-search interval, `values[mid] < target`. Why is `left = mid + 1` the useful update?
questions.explanation: Sorted order proves that indices through mid cannot contain the target. Moving to mid + 1 discards only impossible candidates and strictly shrinks the interval.
hints: The update must satisfy two jobs: preserve possible answers and make the interval smaller.

error_codes.description: The selected reason does not capture both invariant preservation and progress.

source_refs.title: Cornell CS 2112 — Loop invariants

choice_feedback.both: Correct: the update is justified by sorted order and also guarantees progress.
choice_feedback.style: This is a correctness/progress requirement, not a style preference.
choice_feedback.skip: The midpoint is not skipped arbitrarily; it has been proven too small.
choice_feedback.runtime: It does not make the loop constant time.

choices.label: It removes only candidates proven too small and guarantees the interval shrinks
It is only the conventional coding style for binary search
It skips an arbitrary midpoint to make the code faster
It makes the remaining loop O(1)

questions.prompt: For `values = [2, 5, 8, 12, 19]` and `target = 12`, order the search states for the standard inclusive binary search.
questions.explanation: The first midpoint is index 2 with value 8, so the target must be to the right. The interval becomes [3,4]; midpoint 3 is value 12, so the search succeeds.
hints: Compute the midpoint of [0,4], apply the comparison, then compute the midpoint of the remaining interval.

error_codes.description: The candidate interval trace is out of order.

questions.prompt: A function returns the first index of `target` in a list, or `-1` if absent. Which FOUR tests give strong boundary/no-solution coverage?
questions.explanation: Empty input, a match at the first position, duplicate matches, and an absent target probe distinct boundary or contract behaviors. A typical middle match is useful too, but it is the normal case rather than one of the requested boundary/no-solution cases.
hints: Look for minimum size, boundary position, duplicate behavior, and no-solution behavior.

error_codes.description: One boundary/no-solution test was omitted.
A non-boundary item was selected.
The selected set does not cover the requested boundary/no-solution behaviors.

questions.explanation: Boundary tests probe minimal/extreme positions, normal tests probe ordinary behavior, and no-solution tests verify the documented failure result.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the compact correctness checklist for a loop.
questions.explanation: The standard invariant reasoning checks initialization, maintenance, progress toward termination, and what invariant + exit imply. These are separate questions; average-case speed is not part of the correctness proof.
hints: Start before the first iteration; finish by connecting loop exit to the desired result.

error_codes.description: At least one correctness step was misplaced.
At least one correctness step was missing.

pieces.label: Initialization: invariant is true before the loop
Maintenance: one iteration preserves the invariant
Progress: a measure moves toward termination
Exit: invariant + loop exit imply the result
Average case: benchmark a typical machine

questions.prompt: A log processor scans entries left to right. Before processing entry `i`, `error_count` stores the number of ERROR entries already processed. Which invariant best captures that state without relying on the surface story?
questions.explanation: The reusable structure is a processed-prefix invariant: the maintained state exactly summarizes the portion already processed. This same reasoning applies far beyond log processing.

error_codes.description: The selected statement does not express the processed-prefix invariant.

source_refs.title: Cornell CS 2112 — Loop invariants

choice_feedback.prefix: Correct: it precisely connects maintained state to the processed prefix.
choice_feedback.future: The invariant cannot depend on entries that have not been processed.
choice_feedback.positive: The count may be zero; positivity is not the structural rule.
choice_feedback.final: Before the scan finishes, the maintained count need not equal the final count.

choices.label: `error_count` equals the number of ERROR entries among entries before index i
`error_count` includes all future ERROR entries too
`error_count` is always greater than zero
`error_count` always equals the final answer before the scan finishes
